scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): a recommendation response that backs research serving the many while defending basic research and the few; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose at about 400 words on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: There is never enough money or time to study everything researchers might wish to explore.
Some people recommend that scientists and researchers should focus on areas likely to benefit the greatest number of people.
I agree that research should often serve the many, but I believe focusing only on the greatest number would harm science and neglect those in need.

sections.role: Body 1 — Why serving the many is wise

sentences.text: First, directing research toward the greatest benefit is often a wise and fair use of resources.
When money is limited, it makes sense to study problems that affect millions of lives.
For example, research into common diseases like malaria can save far more lives than work on a very rare condition.
This shows that aiming at widespread benefit can do an enormous amount of good.
Such a focus also helps justify the public money that pays for much important research.
Choosing projects by how many people they help can guide limited effort toward the greatest impact.
For these reasons, serving the greatest number is a worthy goal for much research.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why it cannot be the only aim

sentences.text: Second, however, focusing only on the greatest number would damage science in serious ways.
Much basic research seems useless at first, yet later leads to discoveries that help everyone.
Consider how curiosity-driven study of electricity, with no obvious benefit, eventually transformed the entire world.
Such examples show that we cannot always predict which research will prove most valuable.
Counting heads would also abandon small groups, such as people with rare diseases, who deserve help too.
Important knowledge is sometimes worth pursuing for its own sake, not only for immediate numbers.
Research, then, should serve the many without ignoring curiosity or the few.
In conclusion, aiming research at the greatest number of people often does great good.
But focusing on numbers alone would stifle basic discovery and neglect those in greatest need.
The wisest approach balances broad benefit with curiosity and care for small but important groups.
